name: Robert Castellino

essence.line: Fifty years of waiting for the light.
essence.purpose: Hold Colorado still long enough that people see it the way it actually is — in the hour before the day decides what it will be.
essence.promise: Every plate is a real place, made by one man who stood there at dawn, and signed by his own hand.
doList: Name the real place and the real hour
Let the light be the subject
Speak as one maker, first person
Treat the book as an heirloom, not a product
dontList: Borrowed quotes instead of his voice

cta: Signed copies ship from the Boulder studio.
ctaBold: Signed copies ship from the Boulder studio — don't wait on this one.

vlines.playful: Up before the sun for this one.
vlines.bold: Stop here a second — this one earns it.
vlines.formal: A quiet morning, held still long enough to be looked at twice.

messages.text: Before the day decides what it will be
captions: The valleys are still holding the night's cold. For a few minutes the whole state is waiting — and so am I. Pages from Colorado: Life & Light on the Land.
There's an hour before sunrise when nothing has decided yet. That's the hour I drive up the pass for.
I don't chase light. I wait for it, in the dark, with the coffee going cold.

messages.text: Grace comes over the ridge — unearned, unhurried
captions: It comes over a ridge the way grace does: unearned, unhurried, and gone before you can close your hand around it.
Fifty years in, the light still arrives like it means it. My only job is to stay out of its way.
Some mornings the light is offered. I just happen to be standing there, awake, with a camera.

messages.text: A real place you can drive to
captions: No Name Lake, Flat Tops Wilderness. Every plate in the book is a real place in this state — you could stand where I stood.
This isn't a composite. It's a morning, at a named place, on a dated day.
Maroon Bells, Deerlodge Park, Cottonwood Pass — the book is a map of mornings.
headlines: A real place in this state

messages.text: Fifty seconds of light on the Bells
captions: Aspen Snowmass, September. A slow lake, an early frost, and the Bells lit for about fifty seconds.
The storms cleared at 18:42. The peaks held the light for less than a minute. Plate 041.
Red Mountain Pass made a bowl of snow, and a single tree decided to stand in it.
headlines: Lit for less than a minute

messages.text: One man, fifty years, every plate
captions: One photographer. Fifty years of Colorado. Every one of the 84 plates made by waiting for the light.
A 1991 workshop with National Geographic's Sam Abell changed the way I see. The discipline came from The Artist's Way.
No team, no drone fleet, no stock. One man who kept getting up before dawn.

messages.text: Signed by hand from the Boulder studio
captions: Every copy is signed by Robert himself and shipped from the Boulder studio, usually within three business days.
I sign each one by hand. It ships from Boulder. That's the whole supply chain.
A signed first-name hello from the man who made the pictures.
11 × 11, cloth-bound, smyth-sewn, 157gsm archival matte. Built to be handed down, not thrown away.
This is an object, not a feed. Cloth boards, sewn signatures, paper that will outlast all of us.
The kind of book that sits on the table for thirty years and still opens flat.
116 pages. 84 plates. First printing — every copy signed and numbered, with a certificate of authenticity.
Colorado: Life & Light on the Land — the first printing of a fifty-year record.
A 116-page volume of one state, one maker, one lifetime of mornings.

messages.text: A morning you can hang in your home
captions: Some mornings deserve a wall, not a page. Archival pigment prints, made to last a lifetime.
Take one plate off the page and put it where you'll see it every morning.
The Flat Tops at first light — on your wall, at the size the light deserves.
headlines: Off the page, onto the wall

messages.text: Archival pigment prints, made to last
captions: Archival pigment on cotton rag, signed, editioned. Made in Colorado to outlast the frame.
Gallery-grade prints of the plates collectors ask about most.
Museum-grade pigment, hand-signed, shipped flat from Boulder.

assets.title: Cover · Life & Light
assets.blurb: 116 pages, 84 plates, first printing — the cover plate.

assets.title: The morning desk
assets.blurb: Coffee going cold, the day's light being answered one email at a time.

assets.title: The book at the cabin
assets.blurb: The book where it belongs — on a table, in the morning, open.

assets.title: The truck at dawn
assets.blurb: Fifty years of getting up before the sun, one pass at a time.

assets.title: On the coffee table
assets.blurb: Where the book lives for thirty years and still opens flat.

assets.title: The book, evening light
assets.blurb: Cloth boards and sewn signatures, in the last of the day's light.

assets.title: Signed copy, detail
assets.blurb: A signed first-name hello from the man who made the pictures.

assets.title: Metal print, on the wall
assets.blurb: A morning you can hang — archival, signed, made to last.

assets.title: Cascade Creek Falls
assets.blurb: A short walk in, a long wait at the bottom. The light through the spruce was the photograph, not the water.

assets.title: Havasu Creek Cascade
assets.blurb: The water carries calcium carbonate; the calcium carbonate carries the color. The cascades belong to the chemistry as much as to the rock.

assets.title: Havasu, Sunrise
assets.blurb: Ten miles in, an early start, and a window of light that opens for about eleven minutes a year. This was one of them.

assets.title: Latourell Falls
assets.blurb: Two hundred and twenty-four feet of falling water and a basalt cliff that has been waiting underneath it for fifteen million years.

assets.title: Latourell Falls, Vertical
assets.blurb: A second visit, a vertical frame, and the moss on the south wall finally lit.

assets.title: McCloud River, Middle Falls
assets.blurb: The river drops three times in a mile. The middle drop is the one most photographers walk past on the way to the third.

assets.title: McCloud River, the Middle Fall
assets.blurb: Spring runoff, an overcast sky, and an exposure long enough to flatten the spray into a single soft sheet.

assets.title: Mohawk Lake Falls
assets.blurb: Above eleven thousand feet, where the snowmelt is still ice in the shaded pockets and the falls roar for about six weeks a year.

assets.title: Multnomah Falls
assets.blurb: The most photographed waterfall in the Northwest. I arrived at first light, before the parking lot, and had it to myself for forty minutes.

assets.title: Three Rivers Junction, Hot Springs
assets.blurb: Geothermal water meeting cold runoff at sunrise. The steam is the photograph; the rivers are the supporting cast.

assets.title: Travertine Steps, Havasu
assets.blurb: The mineral terraces are remade by every flood. The version photographed here lasted, I am told, about four more years.

assets.title: Carter Lake, Sunrise
assets.blurb: Wind drops at first light for about eleven minutes. This frame was made in the third of them.

assets.title: Carter Lake, Standing Light
assets.blurb: The same lake, a different morning. The cottonwoods on the far shore are the same trees, photographed twenty years apart.

assets.title: Greenlee Pond, Sunrise
assets.blurb: A small pond most maps do not name. The sky did all the work — the pond was simply willing to repeat it.

assets.title: Maroon Bells, Summer's End
assets.blurb: An early frost, a slow lake, and the most photographed peaks in Colorado deciding, briefly, to cooperate.

assets.title: Maroon Bells, Vertical
assets.blurb: Same morning, vertical frame. The reflection runs deeper than the peaks rise; the photograph is half made of water.

assets.title: Causeway Lake, Panoramic
assets.blurb: Eighteen by thirty-six inches in print. Three exposures stitched, made in the order they were composed.

assets.title: Smith Rock, Reflection
assets.blurb: The Crooked River does what its name suggests. The rock face does what the river requires.

assets.title: Tetons, Jackson Lake
assets.blurb: A piece of heart-shaped driftwood at the foreground edge. I did not place it; I waited until the wind did.

assets.title: Walden Ponds II
assets.blurb: Restored wetland on what used to be a gravel quarry. A reminder that some landscapes are recoverable.

assets.title: Walden Ponds, Panoramic
assets.blurb: Three frames stitched. The cattails on the right are the same cattails on the left of the next frame.

assets.title: Walden Ponds, Standard
assets.blurb: A single frame, made the morning after a long night of rain. The light arrived twelve minutes late.

assets.title: Wetlands, Sunrise
assets.blurb: Five degrees and a wind that died at six fifty-two. The frame was composed at six fifty-three.

assets.title: Bat Ray, Scorpion Bay
assets.blurb: Three feet of water, a passing ray, and a polarizer that turned the surface into glass.

assets.title: Boardwalk to the Atlantic
assets.blurb: An old boardwalk and a dune that has, in fifty years, moved nine yards inland.

assets.title: Columbia Gorge, Panoramic
assets.blurb: The river cut through the basalt for fifteen thousand years to leave what you are looking at.

assets.title: Columbia Gorge, Vertical
assets.blurb: A vertical answer to the panoramic — the sky doing the work the river usually claims.

assets.title: Crab in Sand
assets.blurb: Three inches across. The composition is what the crab decided.

assets.title: El Arco at Sunrise
assets.blurb: The famous arch, the famous beach, photographed at the only hour they are willing to be photographed without a crowd.

assets.title: Lone Leaf in Sand
assets.blurb: A leaf the tide put down. The frame is the time between the tide putting it there and the wind taking it away.

assets.title: Milky Way, Haleakalā
assets.blurb: Ten thousand feet up, no moon, twenty-five seconds. Most of what is in the frame is older than the mountain.

assets.title: Milky Way over the Observatory
assets.blurb: The observatories look up; the photograph looks at them looking. A small frame of human attention against a much larger one.

assets.title: Potato Harbor, Sunset
assets.blurb: A two-mile walk from the dock. The last ferry leaves at four; the light was made at six forty-one.

assets.title: Princeville Overlook
assets.blurb: Hanalei Bay from above. The rain on the windward side made the frame; the lee side gave me the light.

assets.title: Skiff, Hanalei Harbor
assets.blurb: One boat, one rope, and a tide that turned during the exposure.

assets.title: Starfish, Tide Pool
assets.blurb: Low tide on a clear morning. The starfish was the third I checked. The light was on the second.

assets.title: Sunset, Henry's Beach
assets.blurb: The cliff behind me holds about fifteen minutes of last light. This was made in the eleventh of them.

assets.title: Tide Pools to Heaven
assets.blurb: A long exposure of the receding tide. The pools held the sky long enough to be looked at twice.

assets.title: Anderson Hole, Yampa
assets.blurb: The Yampa is the last undammed major river in the Colorado system. The light there knows it.

assets.title: Aspen in the Mist
assets.blurb: A cold front, a warm valley, and a half hour when the trees looked like they were standing in their own breath.

assets.title: Bryce, Sunrise Point II
assets.blurb: A second composition from the same overlook. The hoodoos are different photographs at every five degrees of azimuth.

assets.title: Bryce, Sunset Point at Sunrise
assets.blurb: The light at Sunset Point is, in winter, best in the morning. The naming was done by surveyors, not by photographers.

assets.title: Bryce in Winter, Sunrise
assets.blurb: Snow on the hoodoos for about eleven days a year. This was one of them.

assets.title: Cliff Palace
assets.blurb: Eight hundred years of stonework. The photograph is sixty seconds.

assets.title: Delicate Arch in Fog
assets.blurb: The arch is photographed eleven thousand times a year. Fog removes the eleven thousand and leaves the arch.

assets.title: Dream Lake
assets.blurb: A short hike, an early start, and a lake that earns its name about three mornings a season.

assets.title: Fall Colors, Water Knob
assets.blurb: The Smokies do something Colorado cannot: they put red, orange, and yellow on the same ridgeline.

assets.title: Half Dome from Glacier Point
assets.blurb: The Ansel Adams view, made on a morning when the dome was lit and the valley was not.

assets.title: Park Avenue, Wildflowers
assets.blurb: Spring on the slickrock. The flowers last six days; the slickrock has been there one hundred and fifty million years.

assets.title: Hoodoos in Winter
assets.blurb: The snow stays on the north faces and not on the south. The shadow is half the photograph.

assets.title: Kiva, Mesa Verde
assets.blurb: A round stone room. The Ancestral Puebloans understood light from below; the photograph is borrowed from them.

assets.title: Klondike Buttes
assets.blurb: A long dirt road, a longer wait, and a band of last light that crossed the buttes in under two minutes.

assets.title: Mesa Arch, Winter, Vertical
assets.blurb: The arch holds about ninety seconds of fire-orange underglow before the sun clears it. Vertical frame, second visit.

assets.title: Mesa Arch, Winter
assets.blurb: Horizontal frame, same morning. The other photographers had left an hour earlier for breakfast.

assets.title: Park Avenue
assets.blurb: The walk between the walls is the photograph; the walls are simply doing their job.

assets.title: Queen's Garden
assets.blurb: Down into the canyon, then back up. The light at the bottom is the light at the top, half an hour late.

assets.title: Queen's Garden Trail
assets.blurb: The trail itself, made in late morning when the shadows are short and the rock is honest.

assets.title: Reflecting Pool, Zion
assets.blurb: The Virgin River doing what rivers do, photographed at the only hour the canyon walls allow.

assets.title: Water Knob Ridge, Panoramic
assets.blurb: Five frames stitched. The blue ridges are atmosphere, not paint; the haze is the park's namesake.

assets.title: Rim Trail, Fairyland
assets.blurb: Fairyland is the least crowded section of the rim. There is a reason; the photograph is the reason.

assets.title: Turret Arch through North Window
assets.blurb: An arch framed by an arch. Photographed in winter, when the second arch is empty of tourists.

assets.title: Virgin River, Reflect Pools
assets.blurb: The trail to the Emerald Pools, photographed below them — where the water has already done its falling.

assets.title: Water Knob Road
assets.blurb: A road that turns east and then south, photographed at the turn.

assets.title: Mid Pool, Sunset
assets.blurb: The middle pool of the Emerald Pools at last light. The cliff behind it is in red; the water is in blue.

assets.title: Mid Pool, Reflecting Vista
assets.blurb: Same pool, different hour. The cliff is doing the same work; only the light is moving.

assets.title: Autumn, Maroon Bells
assets.blurb: The classic vertical of the Bells in fall — the plate that opens the poster series.

assets.title: Maroon & Pyramid
assets.blurb: Two peaks, one frame, and the air between them lit for under a minute.

assets.title: Maroon & Pyramid, Vertical
assets.blurb: Same peaks, vertical frame. The sky above them is the third subject.

assets.title: Flatirons in Winter Mist
assets.blurb: A morning when the fog held the lower meadow and the sun cleared the rock above it.

assets.title: Hanging Lake, Sparkling Water
assets.blurb: The travertine deposits make the water as photogenic as the cliff behind it. A short hike, a long composition.

assets.title: Behind the Falls
assets.blurb: Standing behind the curtain of water — the photograph the postcards leave out.

assets.title: Lone Pine, Horizontal
assets.blurb: A horizontal frame of the same pine I have photographed for six winters. The composition arrived in the seventh.

assets.title: Old Mine, Red Mountain Pass
assets.blurb: An abandoned mine head, photographed in the same hour as the lone pine. The pass holds more than one photograph.

assets.title: Lone Pine, Vertical
assets.blurb: The vertical companion. Same tree, same hour, different argument.

assets.title: Evening Deer, Trail Ridge
assets.blurb: Twelve thousand feet, last light, and a herd that paused long enough for one exposure.

assets.title: Lake Isabelle, Potentilla
assets.blurb: Yellow shrub-cinquefoil at the foreground edge. Six feet from the camera, doing all the work.

assets.title: Lake Isabelle, Horizontal
assets.blurb: The horizontal answer. The same flowers, photographed from one step to the right.

assets.title: Devil's Thumb Pass, Sunrise
assets.blurb: The thumb of granite the pass is named for, lit first because it sits highest.

assets.title: Wetlands Sunrise
assets.blurb: A small wetland east of the Front Range. The sky is the photograph; the water repeats it.

assets.title: Rainbow over Dallas Divide
assets.blurb: A rainbow lasts about three minutes; the wait was four hours. The arithmetic of this work, on a typical day.

assets.title: Yankee Boy Basin
assets.blurb: Twelve thousand feet of wildflowers, in a basin that opens for about three weeks each summer.

assets.title: Yankee Boy Basin, Horizontal
assets.blurb: The horizontal frame — the basin's full width and the peaks above it.

assets.title: Spring Flatirons
assets.blurb: The meadow in green, the rock in red, and the sky doing the editing.

assets.title: Road Less Traveled
assets.blurb: A dirt road on a high mesa, photographed from where the road ends. The title is honest, for once.

assets.title: Wave, Big Beach
assets.blurb: A single wave at last light. The shape arrived for the duration of a thirtieth of a second.
